examples.label: Example · The 40 m² roof, step by step

body.t: Usable area 40 m² × ~0.20 kW per m² (modern panels at 1,000 W/m² test sunlight) ≈ 8 kW capacity. At 4.5 peak sun hours: ~36 kWh/day, ~13,100 kWh/year at the panels — before inverter, shade and weather losses, which real quotes then deduct.

At mid-latitudes a south-facing tilt near latitude angle is ideal; east or west roofs typically yield ~15–20% less, a flat roof a bit less again, and north-facing (northern hemisphere) drops steeply. The estimate's orientation factor carries these rules of thumb openly.

faq: Can I skip the site survey and order from this number?
Please don't. The estimate screens roofs and sense-checks quotes; ordering needs measured dimensions, a structural once-over and a shading survey. Roofs are expensive to be wrong about.
Which costs and losses stay outside the estimate?

Tariffs and export rates, battery storage, scaffolding, roof repairs and your usage pattern — plus inverter and soiling losses a survey quantifies. The estimate is generation potential, not a bill forecast.
How accurate is the yearly figure?
Order-of-magnitude honest: expect a real system's yield within roughly ±20–25% of the estimate, weather and shade permitting.
The day's sunlight expressed as hours at full 1,000 W/m² strength — Chicago averages around 4–4.5; Phoenix around 6.5; London around 2.5–3. Your region's figure drives the estimate hard.
Common and fine: two smaller arrays facing east and west give a flatter day of generation at a modest total discount versus pure south.
No — storage sizing follows your usage pattern, not the roof. The estimate stops at generation potential, deliberately.
Shade and structure dominate everything else; a shaded 60 m² roof loses to a clear 30 m² one. Get the shading surveyed before believing any number, this page's included.
